BURIAL AND REsCUE.-The Plain Dealer

an interesting incident that occurred re-
Gently in coal mine at, or near Hubbard,
Trumbull county:


Itappears that Hubbard mine is entered
from the river bank, the entrance guarded
by dam. This dam gave way while all
the miners were at dinner except the
four unfortunate ones who were only res
cued yesterday morning. The four men
comprehending their situation fled to the
highest portion of the mine, at about a
halt mile from the entrance. Their fellow
wOrkmen outside, supposing they would
seek this point, commenced Immediately
over it, as near as they could judge, and
after penetrating sixty-eight feet tortu-
nately struck the pit in close proximity to
two of the half-famished men. BY means
of a tube they were enabled to communi-
cate with them and give them food. Of the
other two no information could be OBJ
tained. The scene about the pit until, and
at their rescue was very affecting. All
were married and their wives and children
never left the pit till their deliverance.-
Yesterday morning the water in the river
had so fallen as to admit small boat and
two men, who, after entering the pit about
half mile, found two of the men speechless
with exhaustion, and few rods further
they found the other two, and brought all
safe to the open air. The scene can better
be imagined than described. About two
thousand people were present at the time.
The men were with difficulty resuscitated,
but are now doing well.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 1.-THE ex-Chief of
the Fox tribe had an interview with the
Commissioner Of Indian Affairs this fore
noon,in relation to their material interests.
The Sacs and Foxes have already reserva-
tion in Kansas and an annuity of SOL, 200,
but the Foxes will not live with the Sacs,
and have located in Kansas, and now want
the Government to change arrangements

asked, among other things, how they would
like to 60 into the Indian Territory, where
it was proposed to establish govern
ment, embracing many of the Indian
tribes, but they said they wanted to think
all matters over. They had always been
good friends to onr Government and peo-
ple. When, however, they came to talk
with their white father, there was always
something harsh. This was wrong, They
could get along better with smooth and
easy words. They wanted to see their
white father, the President. ~ u'Gr- =


The Commissioner replied that If the
Foxes ran away from their reservation and
discarded the treaty, all advantages would
inure to the Sacs. They must go back, or
give some good reason why they do not re-
turn.

for them to live with the Sacs. They were
to have another talk with the Commissioner
and were promised sight OF the white
father before they left Washington.

New YORK, March 1l.-Another batch
of Union prisoners from the slaughter pens
arrived this morning. The men belong in
the upper part of New York State, and
have been absent from their friends and
families over three years. These men, all
of whom have improved in appearance
since they have been exchanged, expressed
themselves in most bitter terms against the
treatment they received from the rebel au-
thorities. At Andersonville the men were
so reduced in flesh from the unwholesome
food which they were forced to eat or starve,
that sores broke out on their bodies.


In the battles before Richmond last spring
they were taken prisoners, and have been in
close confinement nearly one year. A fur
lough of thirty days has been extended to
them, after which they will return to the
front and rejoin their regiments.

text:
WASHINGTON, March 4-President Lin
coin was inauguratedl at II o'clok noon to-
day. The weather was clear and beautiful,
but on account of recent rains the streets
were filled with mud. Despite this fact the
crowd that assembled was exceedingly
large, and thousands proceeded to the Cap
itol to witness the inauguration ceremonies.


The first dispatch stated that the process
sion formed while heavy rain was falling. j
The procession moved from Sixteenthstreet
and Pennsylvania Avenue at II o'clock
President Lincoln had been at the Capitol
all day, and consequently did not accom-
pany the procession to the scene of the cere-
monies. Two regiments of the Invalid
Corps, a squadron of cavalry, battery of
artillery and four companies OF colored
troops, formed the military escort. The
Mayor and Councilmen of Washington,
Councilmen from Baltimore, the firemen of
this city and from Philadelphia, the Good
will, Franklina and Perseverance companies,
each company drawing its engine along,
were also in the procession. Among the
benevolent societies present were lodges
of Odd Fellows and Masons, includ-
ing cOlored lodge of the latter fra
ternity. The public and principal private
buildings on Pennsylvania avenue were
galy decorated with flags, and every
window was thronged with faces to catch
glimpse of the President elect.


The oath to protectand maintain the Con-
stitution of the United States was admins
tered to Mr.. Lincoln by Chief Justice Chase,
In presence of thousands who witnessed the
Interesting ceremony, while standing in
mud almost knee deep. The inaugural
was then read, upon which national salute
was fired. The procession then again mov-
ed up PENNSYLVANIA avenue, the President
being conveyed in an open barouch. Seated
with him was his son and Senator Foster,
of the committee of Arrangements. The
President was escorted to the White House,
after which the procession separated.


Everything passed off ina most quiet and
orderly manner, and although thousands
participated in the ceremonies not one acci-
dent occurred to mar the pleasures of the
day.

and daughter of Mrs. Blye, residing short
distance from that place, came to her death
in the following melancholy manner:


ltappears that on the above evening, at
ter Mrs. Blye had put her young children
to bed, she left the house to call on some OF
her neighbors, and left her Oldest daughter
to care for the same in her absence. Short
" after the mother was gone she procured
her knitting and lamp, which she placed
between her knees, and worked at her
stocking until she fell asleep, during which
time fire was communicated tO'her clothes.
She did not awake until she was complete
" wrapped in flames, and finding herself
in this condition she became alarmed, and
ran out of the house crying for help, when

but not until every thread of her garments
were burned off her body. She was taken
into the house, and everything done to re-
lieve her of her misery, but all to no effect.

death relieved her of all her suffering. Let

WASHINGTON, May Pal p. M-The city
was much crowded to-day; weather de-
| lightful. The armies of Tennessee and
Georgia were reviewed by Lieutenant Cen
eral Grant. The President and members
of the Cabinet, distinguished army and
navy officers and others occupied the stands

umn, and was heartily cheered all along

plimcnted. The military display was

SECOND DISPATCH.


WASHINGTON, May 2i.-We had another
bright day for the review. Fresh arrivals
this morning augmented the already large
numbt + of strangers who had visited WASH
ington to witness the grand military parade.
| The tastefully decorated stands near the
Executive Mansion were again occupied by
President johnson, members of the Cabinet,
and Lieut.. Gen. Grant and other distin-
guished army and navy officers, Chiefs Of

| ing the most attractive.





the Capitol at 8 A. NJ, proceeding toward

was cheered all along the line. The greet

terday assumed command of this army

flags waved.

general sameness of uniforms, and several

duce the effect. Sections of pontoon

procession. There was also a fair represen-
tation of the spade and axe department,
the Implements being carried on the should
ers of white and black soldiers. Much
amusement was occasioned by dis
play of pack horses and mules. They
were all heavily loaded with COM
missary supplies, including chickens; a
COW, a dog and goat were comfort
ably fastened to the saddles. These were
the spoils of the soldiers. Two black sol.
diers of the largest size riding very small
mules, their feet nearly touching the ground
was regarded as comic scene in connection
with this part of the display, and occasionet
general laughter. u.


An interesting feature in the parade wa
the exhibition of flags and banners of va
rious regiments, some of them entirely
new; Others were carried torn by bullet
and reduced to shreds while others, made
of stronger MATERIAL were faded by eX
posure to the weather or blackened by thu
smoke of battle. Some staffs were carried
from which the flags had been shot away
All the spear-heads were adorned with flags


1t was remarked as in contrast to tht
Army of the Potomac, that the troops com
prising the Armies of Georgia and Tennes
see wore the wide brim felt hats, regulation
pattern. Their appearance in all respects
was equal to that of the Potomac army
and Notwithstanding they had performed
more marching service, their movement
were much admired and applauded.


The commander of each Army and Corps
and Division, attended by one staff officer
dismounted after passing the General-in
Chief and joined him until his Army Corp
or Division had passed the reviewing
stand, when he joined his command.


Brigade bands or consolidated field mu


sic turned out and played as their brigade'


passed. One band of each division per


formed during the march from the Capito


to the Treasury building. After the troop
passed the Treasury building they wer


marched to their respective quarters.


Secretary Seward, Notwithstanding hi


severe physical afliction, took deep in


terest in the review Gen. Augur mad
him comfortable and furnished him with


good position at the headquarters of the de


fenses of Washington, that he might wit
ness the grand military spectacle.
The armies of Tennessee and Georgia oc
. cupied six hours in passing, the same lengt
! of time required yesterday for the review Q
the army Of the Potomac.

How grandly the columns stretched away,

Never again in the worlds sunlight,

Their lifelong battles and marches DER, q

of the james correspondent says: All in
camp except the General himself appeared
greatly surprised at his removal. If the re-
moval was caused by the Wilmington fail
ure, it was inquired why it was not sooner
made. The answer to this was that Gen
Ord, who temporarily succeeds Gen. Butler,
was absent, and the authorities only await
ed his return. Gen. Butler received the or
der about half past eleven Sunday forenoon,
and before three in the afternoon had made
all his farewell preparations, turned over
the army to his successor, and taken his de-
parture for the North.

says the inhabitants are suffering from
scarcity of food. and the rebel troops are
quartered upon them, rendering their con-
dition still more deplorable. No new active
military movements of importance have
taken place recently in the valley.
